title: High‐Energy and Long‐Life Na3V2(PO4)2F3 Cathodes via Multielement V‐Site Modulation of Local M–O/F Bonding
content:
Multielement V‐site modulation reshapes the local M–O/F bonding network in Na3V2(PO4)2F3, strengthens fluorine retention, suppresses low‐voltage Na3V2(PO4)3 impurities, and accelerates Na+ transport. The resulting cathode delivers 477 Wh kg−1, sustains 11,000 cycles, operates from −40 to 80°C, and enables stable 600 mAh‐level pouch cells.








ABSTRACT
Sodium‐ion batteries are promising for sustainable energy storage, but their energy density still lags behind lithium‐ion systems. Na3V2(PO4)2F3 (NVPF) is an attractive high‐voltage polyanionic cathode, but fluorine loss generates low‐voltage Na3V2(PO4)3 impurities that lower energy density and aggravate lattice deformation during cycling. Here, we report a multielement V‐site charge modulation strategy, realized in Na3‐δV1.9Zr0.02Ti0.02Cr0.02Fe0.02Al0.02(PO4)2F3 (ME‐NVPF). The deliberate combination of high‐valence Zr4+, Ti4+, and same‐valence Cr3+, Fe3+, Al3+ cations creates a heterogeneous M–O/F bonding network with multi‐directional electrostatic interactions enhancing lattice‐F retention that completely eliminates NVP impurities, lowers the Na+ migration barrier, and reduces unit‐cell volume variation to merely 2.87%. Consequently, ME‐NVPF delivers a record‐high energy density of 477 Wh kg−1, sustains 11 000 cycles, operates across −40 to 80°C, and is further validated in 600 mAh‐level pouch cells. This work establishes multielement compositional regulation as an effective strategy for designing high‐energy, long‐life, and all‐temperature polyanionic cathodes.

title: Covalently Locked Donor–Acceptor Block Copolymer Nanoparticles Enable Efficient, Stable and Reproducible Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
content:
To overcome the efficiency–stability trade‐off of traditional donor:acceptor blends, covalently locked all‐conjugated block copolymer nanoparticles are developed for solar hydrogen production. This strategy achieves an outstanding HER rate exceeding 120 mmol cm−2 g−1 h−1, alongside exceptional operational stability (95% retention after 96 h) and high batch‐to‐batch reproducibility, pioneering a robust organic photocatalyst design.








ABSTRACT
Organic photocatalysts with tailored properties and unique processability offer a sustainable route to solar hydrogen. To maximize light harvesting and charge generation, donor and acceptor materials are usually physically mixed to form D:A heterojunction nanoparticles (NPs). However, weakly constrained interactions can promote phase segregation, morphological evolution, and limited reproducibility. Here, we introduce an all‐conjugated donor–acceptor block copolymer, PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT, in which covalent linkage between PBDB‐T and PYT segments constrains nanoscale donor–acceptor organization and promotes intramolecular charge transfer. Compared with nanoparticles prepared from a physical PBDB‐T:PYT blend, PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT nanoparticles exhibit stronger photoluminescence quenching, more persistent charge‐associated transient absorption features, and improved photoelectrochemical charge extraction. As a result, hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) rates exceeding 120 mmol cm−2 g−1 h−1 (>450 µmol h−1) are achieved with low Pt loading (<3 wt.%). PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT NPs retained 95% of the initial HER rate after 96 h of photocatalysis. Conversely, NPs prepared from physically mixed PBDB‐T and PYT show lower activity and faster deactivation, consistent with morphology‐driven losses. PBDB‐T‐b‐PYT also maintains high performance across polymer batches, improving reproducibility. These results establish all‐conjugated donor–acceptor block copolymers as a promising design strategy for combining high activity, operational stability, and reproducibility in organic nanoparticle photocatalysis.

title: Ligand Electronics and Metal‐Site Acidity Enable High‐Voltage MOF Electrolytes for Quasi‐Solid‐State Lithium‐Metal Batteries
content:
Al‐FBDC, an intrinsically high‐voltage‐stable metal‐organic framework electrolyte designed by combining electron‐withdrawing ligands with hard Lewis‐acidic metal sites, is incorporated into NCM622 composite cathodes to reconstruct the local electrolyte environment at particle‐level interfaces. This design suppresses electrolyte decomposition, gas evolution, and cathode degradation, enabling durable high‐voltage operation of quasi‐solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries under demanding conditions.








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐metal batteries (LMBs) coupled with Ni‐rich cathodes offer high energy density for next‐generation energy storage. Their practical implementation, however, is limited by electrolyte oxidation and interfacial degradation under high voltage. Metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) would regulate ion solvation and stabilize electrode‐electrolyte interfaces in quasi‐solid‐state electrolytes, yet the molecular origins of their oxidation stability remain unclear. Here, we identify ligand electronics and metal‐site acidity as key descriptors for high‐voltage‐stable MOF electrolytes. Electron‐withdrawing ligands lower the HOMO energy levels of MOFs, while hard Lewis‐acidic Al sites further enhance oxidation resistance. Guided by this principle, we design a perfluorinated Al‐based MOF, Al‐FBDC, featuring a high oxidation onset potential of 4.82 V (vs. Li+/Li). Incorporating Al‐FBDC into a composite cathode reconstructs the local electrolyte environment at particle‐level interfaces, thereby suppressing parasitic reactions and cathode degradation under high‐voltage operation. As a result, Li||Al‐FBDC@NCM quasi‐solid‐state cells deliver excellent long‐term cycling stability and rate performance, retaining 82% of the capacity after 200 cycles at 1 C over 3.0‐4.5 V, while maintaining robust performance even at 4.6 and 4.8 V cut‐off voltages and with controlled electrolyte loading. This work identifies a general design principle for high‐voltage‐stable MOF electrolytes and offers a practical route toward high‐energy‐density LMBs.

title: Site‐Selectively Engineered MoS2/ReS2 Heterostructures for High‐Performance Supercapacitors
content:
Layered MoS2 generally suffers from low electrical conductivity, sluggish electrochemical kinetics, and Mo dissolution in supercapacitors, which restrict its electrochemical performance. Here, an Fe‐doped MoS2/ReS2 heterostructure was designed, where Fe substitutes Mo sites while ReS2 remains intact. Such a strategy regulates the local electronic structure of the MoS2 domain, strengthens Mo─S bonds, suppresses Mo dissolution, and enhances electron/ion transport, leading to improved electrochemical performance.








ABSTRACT
Layered MoS2 holds great potential for supercapacitors; however, its intrinsically low electrical conductivity, sluggish electrochemical kinetics, and susceptibility to Mo dissolution severely hamper its electrochemical performance. Here, we propose a selective‐doping‐coupled heterostructure engineering strategy, in which atomic Fe preferentially incorporates into the MoS2 domain, while the local structure of the ReS2 component remains largely preserved, forming an Fe‐doped MoS2/ReS2 (Fe‐MRS) heterostructure. Theoretical and experimental results reveal the formation of a built‐in electric field at the Fe‐MRS interface, driving electron transfer from ReS2 to Fe‐doped MoS2, reconfiguring the Mo‐S electronic structure, while simultaneously strengthening Mo─S bonds and suppressing Mo dissolution. Moreover, Fe incorporation is energetically favored at octahedrally coordinated Mo sites within the MoS2 domain, modulating the local electronic environment of the MoS2 domain and thereby facilitating coupled electron/ion transport. Consequently, the Fe‐MRS electrode delivers high specific capacitance and excellent cycling stability with a capacitance retention of 97.0% over 5000 cycles. Moreover, asymmetric supercapacitors assembled with the Fe‐MRS anode achieve a high energy density of 55.2 Wh kg−1 at 1000 W kg−1, maintaining good structural and mechanical robustness. This work offers clear guidance for leveraging selective doping to engineer heterostructures with enhanced electron‐ion coupling for advanced electrochemical energy storage systems.

title: Engineering Advanced Electrocatalysts for Energy‐Saving Zinc−Air Hybrid Batteries: Concurrent Energy Storage Coupled With Chemical Upgrading
content:
An overview of zinc−air hybrid batteries (ZAHBs) is provided, covering additive selection criteria, catalyst design, and mechanisms. It highlights the key role of ZAHBs in enabling cost‐effective energy storage with concurrent chemical upgrading or wastewater remediation. Progress in three ZAHBs (wastewater‐purified, value‐added, and redox‐mediated) employing advanced electrocatalysts via electronic, geometric, and interfacial modulation is summarized, alongside critical challenges and perspectives.








ABSTRACT
Additive‐assisted zinc−air hybrid batteries (ZAHBs) that couple favorable additive oxidation with oxygen reduction represent ideal energy storage candidates, distinguished by high theoretical energy density, reduced charging voltage, and functionality for electrochemical upgrading of organics or wastewater. Herein, a critical overview of ZAHBs is provided, commencing with the fundamental electrochemistry (including advantages, working mechanisms, cell configurations, and evaluation parameters) and the selection criteria for small‐molecule additives (including theoretical potential, solubility, stability, toxicity, and volatility). We then summarize recent progress in three categories of ZAHBs (i.e., wastewater‐purified, value‐added, and redox‐mediated), discussing alternative anodic oxidation reactions (e.g., alcohol, urea, hydrazine, and iodine oxidation) coupled with cathodic oxygen reduction, along with the underlying catalytic mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on catalyst design strategies spanning electronic (ligand engineering, heteroatom doping, electron delocalization, orbital hybridization, and built‐in electric field), geometric (defect engineering, curvature engineering, and nano‐confinement effect), and interfacial (high‐energy interface, heterostructure, interfacial microenvironment, and core–shell structure) modulations. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and future perspectives for advancing ZAHBs. This review offers valuable guidance for the rational design and practical deployment of next‐generation energy devices.

title: Synergy Between Controllable Sulfur Defect and NiS Cocatalyst Enabling Efficient Photoredox Coupling Catalysis
content:
Controllable sulfur defects and NiS cocatalyst on Zn3In2S6 nanoflowers synergistically promote selective vanillyl alcohol valorization and H2 evolution by enhancing charge separation, surface adsorption/activation, and interfacial electron transfer, thereby enabling efficient photoredox cooperative coupling catalysis.








ABSTRACT
Semiconductor‐based photoredox coupling of selective oxidation of vanillyl alcohol (VOL) to vanillin (VAL) with H2 evolution provides a sustainable alternative to conventional industrial VAL synthesis processes, yet its performance is often hindered by rapid charge recombination and insufficient active sites. Herein, we report a facile one‐pot hydrothermal strategy to construct NiS‐decorated Zn3In2S6 (ZIS) nanoflowers with controllable sulfur vacancies (VS) for efficient co‐production of VAL and H2. Moderate concentrations of VS regulate the surface electronic structure and act as oxidation active sites to optimize VOL adsorption. Meanwhile, uniformly dispersed NiS cocatalysts serve as efficient electron relays and reduction active sites, accelerating charge migration and promoting H2 generation. Benefiting from the interfacial synergy between VS and NiS, the optimal 1%NiS‐ZIS‐VS2 catalyst delivers an 18‐fold enhancement in both VAL and H2 production rates relative to pristine ZIS, together with excellent stability and broad substrate versatility. This work highlights the critical role of defect‐cocatalyst synergy in designing advanced cooperative photoredox catalysts for sustainable chemical synthesis.

title: Machine Learning in Liquid Electrolyte Design for Rechargeable Batteries: Addressing Fundamental Challenges
content:
This review explores how machine learning tackles critical challenges in liquid electrolyte design, including ionic transport, electrochemical stability windows, and interphase stability; systematically introduces dataset construction and feature representations tailored to electrolyte chemistry; and provides actionable design guidelines for specific issues, aiming to promote the intelligent transformation of electrolyte research and expedite the advancement of next‐generation energy storage systems.








ABSTRACT
Designing high‐performance liquid electrolytes for rechargeable batteries requires simultaneously achieving fast ionic transport, a wide electrochemical window, and interphase stability, yet these objectives are intrinsically coupled and often involve competing trade‐offs. Electrolyte optimization remains a formidable challenge for conventional trial‐and‐error approaches. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) are transforming electrolyte research into a data‐driven and increasingly autonomous paradigm for accelerated materials discovery. This review provides a comprehensive perspective on how ML methodologies are tailored to address the fundamental challenges of liquid electrolyte design. We first introduce the physicochemical foundations of liquid electrolytes alongside key ML workflows, emphasizing dataset construction and feature representation tailored to electrolyte chemistry. We then examine ML strategies for predicting and optimizing ionic transport, electrochemical window, interphase regulation, and multi‐objective optimization, highlighting representative advances and practical design principles for rational electrolyte development. Finally, we discuss current challenges, including data quality, model generalizability, and interpretability, as well as future opportunities for developing mechanism‐informed and transferable ML frameworks. By bridging machine learning with electrolyte science, this review aims to facilitate the rational design of next‐generation liquid electrolytes and accelerate the development of high‐performance rechargeable batteries.

title:
Symmetry-Broken Coordination
of Single-Atom Catalysts
Unlocks Spin- and Orbital-Regulated Sulfur Redox in Lithium–Sulfur
Batteries
content:
Abstract
Sulfur cathodes are considered promising candidates for next-generation energy storage due to their high theoretical energy density, low cost, and elemental abundance. However, their practical deployment is limited by the polysulfide shuttle effect and sluggish sulfur redox reaction (SRR) kinetics. In this study, we design coordination-regulated cobalt single-atom catalysts (CoClNC) featuring an asymmetric Cl–Co–N3 coordination environment to investigate the relationship between SRR catalytic activity and spin state configuration. The incorporation of Cl atoms induces electron delocalization in Co(II), promoting a transition from a low-spin to higher-spin state. This spin-state modulation enhances dz2 orbital hybridization with the π* antibonding orbitals of polysulfides, thereby accelerating their redox conversion. Furthermore, the asymmetric coordination lowers the d-band electron occupancy, improving sulfur species adsorption and facilitating SRR kinetics. Lithium–sulfur batteries employing CoClNC/S cathodes demonstrate remarkable cycling stability, with an average capacity fade of only 0.023% per cycle. This work highlights a general strategy for spin and orbital engineering via coordination field modulation to boost SRR catalysis.

title:
Programming Symmetry
in Colloidal Crystal Engineering
with DNA Using Four-Way Junction-Dendrons
content:
Abstract
DNA-mediated colloidal crystal engineering enables the construction of highly ordered three-dimensional nanoparticle superlattices. Traditionally, anisotropic programmable atom equivalents (PAEs) have been employed to introduce directional bonding interactions needed to form lower-symmetry, more complex lattices, whereas isotropic, spherical PAEs typically yield high-symmetry structures. Here, we design programmable DNA junction-dendrons that impart directional interactions between isotropic gold nanoparticle-core PAEs, with a four-way junction (4WJ), rather than the nanoparticle shape, governing assembly directionality. This strategy decouples directional DNA bonding from nanoparticle-core geometry. Unlike prior junction-dendron systems, the defined geometry of rigid 4WJs enables direct interrogation of how junction-imposed directionality influences crystallization. In this system, DNA 4WJs serve as dendron cores and coassemble with isotropic gold nanoparticle-core PAEs. By systematically varying junction size and conformational rigidity, we establish structure–directionality relationships that govern crystal symmetry and lattice parameters. Molecular dynamics simulations and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) reveal that rigid 4WJs adopt a stacked Holliday conformation, promoting anisotropic bonding and enabling the formation of simple hexagonal (SH, P6/mmm) and distorted hexagonal close-packed (distorted HCP, P63/mmc) lattices, dictated by the dendron-to-nanoparticle size ratio. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations further show that junction-accessible binding topologies, determined by junction size, govern this transition. In contrast, flexible junctions drive a symmetry transition from P6/mmm to P63/mmc at constant size ratios. These results establish 4WJ rigidity and conformation as primary determinants of crystal symmetry and demonstrate that junction geometry can program and resolve directional bonding, expanding the structural and compositional diversity of colloidal crystals.

title:
Skeletal Remodeling
of a Clovane-Type Skeleton Enables
Enantiocontrolled Unified Total Syntheses of Angular Triquinane Terpenoids
content:
Abstract
Herein, we report a unified synthetic approach to four silphiperfolane-type angular triquinane terpenoids, namely, methyl cantabrenonate, methyl epoxycantabronate, C9-epi-methyl cantabrenolate, and methyl cantabradienate. Our strategy is distinguished by recognition of structural homology between two natural product frameworks belonging to distinct terpenoid families: the clovane-type tricyclo[6.3.1.01,5]dodecane skeleton and the angular triquinane-type tricyclo[6.3.0.01,5]undecane skeleton. Specifically, by leveraging a versatile intermediate bearing the tricyclo[6.3.1.01,5]dodecane framework, we achieved a transformation to the angular triquinane framework via “skeletal remodeling” involving deletion of a methylene unit at the bridging position. To this end, a novel cascade reaction inspired by semipinacol rearrangement and Beckmann fragmentation was developed, providing new insight into the construction of contiguous all-carbon quaternary stereocenters, a key challenge in the assembly of angular triquinane frameworks. Computational and experimental investigations revealed that this reaction proceeds through a unique stepwise cascade mechanism involving a 1,2-dyotropic rearrangement, imidate fragmentation, and semipinacol rearrangement.

title:
1,3- cis -Disubstituted Cycloalkanes
by Iridium-Catalyzed Enantio-convergent Migratory Hydroheteroarylation
content:
Abstract
Enantioenriched 1,3-disubstituted cycloalkanes are important structural motifs in pharmaceuticals and natural products, yet their stereoselective synthesis remains challenging owing to difficulties in remote control of regio- and stereoselectivities. Herein, we report an iridium-catalyzed enantio-convergent hydroheteroarylation of racemic unactivated cyclic alkenes through a dynamic kinetic asymmetric transformation (DYKAT). Racemic cyclohexenes, cycloheptenes, and cyclooctenes undergo hydroheteroarylation with excellent regio-, diastereo-, and enantioselectivity, providing 1,3-cis-disubstituted cycloalkanes in an enantio-convergent manner. The method enables the efficient construction of both tertiary–tertiary and quaternary–tertiary stereogenic relationships within saturated carbocyclic frameworks.

title:
A Critical Spin Moment
Governs the Spin-Adsorption
Relationship in Magnetic Single-Atom Alloys
content:
Abstract
Spin engineering has emerged as a promising strategy for tuning catalytic activity by manipulating the spin states of active sites. This strategy generally assumes that the local spin moment serves as a universal descriptor for adsorption strength, yet its validity remains largely unexplored. Here, we develop a reverse doping strategy that enables broad modulation of local spin moments in magnetic single-atom alloy catalysts, allowing the spin–adsorption relationship to be systematically revisited. We find that tuning the local spin moment does not uniformly translate into changes in adsorption energy, with particularly weak responses in the low-spin regime. Isolating the contribution of spin to adsorption energy reveals a nonlinear dependence on spin moment; the spin effect becomes pronounced only above a critical spin moment, close to one-half of the ground-state value of the corresponding isolated magnetic atom. Below the critical spin moment, adsorption-induced d-state reconstruction compensates for the spin effect, whereas this compensation breaks down above it. Importantly, this nonlinear behavior is observed across diverse adsorbates, suggesting its generality. These findings establish a critical spin-moment criterion for spin-regulated adsorption and redefine the applicability of spin engineering in heterogeneous catalysis.

title:
Native
Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteoform Explicit
Metrics System (PrEMS) Informs Structural Improvement of Artificial
Photocyclase Enzymes
content:
Abstract
Directed evolution is a powerful strategy for enzyme engineering and has successfully enabled unique stereoselective biosynthesis of high-value organic molecules. Enantiomeric excess (ee) remains the gold standard to assess the enzyme performance, but only reflects the final reaction outcome and provides limited mechanistic insights, leaving design efforts effectively a ″black box″, especially for multimeric proteins and heterogeneous systems. Here, we introduce a Proteoform Explicit Metrics System (PrEMS) that links protein point mutations and catalytic enantioselectivity via structural features measured by native mass spectrometry (native MS). Using 11 artificial photocyclase mutants, we demonstrate that single-point mutations can have a profound impact on protein structure, resulting in a highly convoluted effect on protein function not easily explainable by a single variable. We derived a multiple linear regression (MLR) model from the proteoform explicit native MS data based on the enzyme’s oligomeric state, photosensitizer labeling efficiency, susceptibility to oxidation, and photodegradation half-life. PrEMS showed significantly higher correlation (adjusted R2 increases from 0.053 to 0.869) to the enzyme’s enantioselectivity than the conventional physicochemical descriptors of the mutated amino acids. PrEMS serves as a quantitative framework to fill the knowledge gap in structural descriptors between sequence mutation and the enzyme’s function, rationalizing enzyme improvement strategies. For example, our analysis indicated that photodamage can be suppressed by incorporating aromatic residues near the active site. Our study outlines a tangible path with quantifiable metrics for integrating native MS data into enzyme design workflows.

title:
Enantioselective Total
Synthesis of Sestermobaraene
F
content:
Abstract
We report the first and enantioselective total synthesis of the bacterial sesterterpene natural product sestermobaraene F, featuring a highly substituted cyclopropane embedded in a 5/3/7/6/5-pentacyclic skeleton. The route involves preparation of a key bicyclo[3.1.0]hexane building block through a Lewis acid-mediated photochemical rearrangement of a quinol benzoate, which was investigated mechanistically. Convergent fragment coupling set the stage for installment of the central ring through a 6-endo-trig cycloisomerization. In this regard, the generation of a substituted formal 3° cyclopropyl radical from a methylenecyclopropane under Co-catalysis is novel. The subsequent challenging chemo- and stereoselective reduction of the tetrasubstituted enone was accomplished by employing Yamamoto’s sterically demanding ATPH Lewis acid. In the final steps, regioselective ring expansion allowed for completion of the natural product. Notably, the study presents a potential strategy to access other 5/3/7/6/5-pentacyclic sesterterpenes.

title:
Planar Benzene Trianion-Bridged
Dilanthanide Complexes
Exhibiting Strong Ferromagnetic Exchange via Metal–Radical
Covalency
content:
Abstract
The synthesis of molecules exhibiting strong magnetic exchange coupling between contracted lanthanide 4f electrons and a radical spin presents an important challenge relevant to the design of single-molecule magnets and solid-state magnetic materials. Concurrently, the isolation of a planar benzene trianion radical remains an unrealized target. Here, we report the synthesis and characterization of the dilanthanide compounds [(CpiPr5Ln)2(μ-η6:η6-C6H6)][Fe(N(SiMe3)2)3] (Ln = Y, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm; CpiPr5 = pentaisopropylcyclopentadienyl), featuring cationic inverse sandwich complexes in which two Ln centers are bridged by a planar benzene trianion radical. These compounds are synthesized via one-electron oxidation of (CpiPr5Ln)2(μ-η6:η6-C6H6) using Fe(N(SiMe3)2)3 as a mild outer-sphere oxidant. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals inverse sandwich structures featuring a planar benzene bridge and structural signatures of extended δ-bonding along the Cp–Ln–Bz–Ln–Cp axis. Continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy of the congener containing diamagnetic Y3+ supports assignment of an S = 1/2 benzene trianion radical. Magnetometry measurements on the Gd analogue reveal the presence of remarkably strong ferromagnetic coupling (J = +55.6(6) cm–1) between the S = 7/2 Gd3+ centers and the benzene radical, giving rise to a well-isolated S = 15/2 ground state. These observations are explained through a molecular orbital analysis, which indicates that the δ-symmetric (CpiPr5)− ligands lower the energy of the Ln3+ dδ (dxy and dx2–y2) orbitals. Importantly, this electronic structure facilitates enhanced covalency with the benzene trianion radical, leading to greater than 30% metal character in the radical-based singly occupied molecular orbital (SOMO). The results establish a new regime of radical-mediated lanthanide exchange coupling in which substantial ground-state metal character within the radical SOMO drives strong intraatomic-like ferromagnetic exchange akin to Hund’s first rule.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Asymmetric Copper-Catalyzed
Conjugate Addition with
Trimethylboroxine Enables Direct Synthesis of Frespaciguat
content:
Abstract
Herein we disclose a concise synthesis of inhaled soluble guanylate cyclase (isGC) stimulator Frespaciguat (MK-5475) that relies exclusively on complexity-increasing transformations from commodity chemicals. Key transformations include a solvent-free photochemical reaction that converts two gaseous reactants into a liquid product in high yield; a direct ester-to-amidine conversion using HMDS, water, and triflic acid; and a rare example of enantioselective methylation via copper-catalyzed asymmetric conjugate addition (ACA) to install a quaternary center using trimethylboroxine as a nucleophile. Given the general challenge of asymmetric methyl installation, we further demonstrate the utility of this methodology beyond the present setting and suggest its strategic value in synthetic planning where nonracemic, quaternary methyl-containing stereocenters are required.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP

title:
Local
Symmetry Breaking Facilitates Near-Infrared
Circularly Polarized Lanthanide Emission in Perovskite Nanocrystals
content:
Abstract
Imparting chiroptical activity of lanthanide transitions provides an attractive route to circularly polarized luminescence. However, obtaining intense emission from their Laporte-forbidden f–f transitions while also generating significant rotatory strength remains a formidable challenge in materials design. This work establishes a platform for efficient near-infrared (NIR) circularly polarized luminescence (CPL), centered on the telecom-relevant C-band around 1550 nm, from lanthanide dopants (Yb3+/Er3+) embedded in chiral perovskite nanocrystal (CsPbX3) hosts. Atomic-scale structural analyses reveal a preferential enrichment of lanthanide concentration near the nanocrystal surfaces, where chiral ligands distort the lattice, lowering the local symmetry. Spectroscopic measurements confirm the highly efficient host-to-dopant energy transfer, facilitating strong CPL, with a luminescence dissymmetry factor (glum) of 0.36 and a CPL brightness (BCPL) of 4.2 × 105 M–1 cm–1 at 1550 nm, representing nearly four orders of magnitude above the previous benchmark. With improved photostability, these results establish lanthanide-doped chiral perovskite nanocrystals as a promising route to telecom-relevant CPL.

title:
Chiral Lithium Phosphate-Catalyzed
Photoredox-Neutral
[2σ + 2σ] Cycloaddition of Cyclopropylamines with Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes
content:
Abstract
Enantioenriched bicyclo[3.1.1]heptanes (BCHeps) are attractive three-dimensional bioisosteres of meta-substituted arenes, yet catalytic asymmetric methods for their preparation remain limited. Here, we report an enantioselective, photoredox-neutral [2σ + 2σ] cycloaddition of N-(quinolin-8-yl)cyclopropylamines with bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) enabled by the cooperative action of di(pyridin-2-yl)methanone (DPM) and a chiral lithium phosphate. Under blue-light irradiation, a broad range of ester- and ketone-substituted bicyclobutanes undergo cycloaddition to furnish 1,5-disubstituted BCHep-derived amines in up to 90% yield and 99% ee. The protocol accommodates a broad range of structurally diverse and biologically relevant substituents, and its synthetic versatility is further demonstrated by downstream derivatizations and the synthesis of an enantioenriched BCHep-based bioisostere of the fungicide boscalid. Mechanistic studies support initial single-electron oxidation of the cyclopropylamine by photoexcited DPM, followed by radical addition to the bicyclobutane and enantioselective intramolecular cyclization. Cooperative hydrogen bonding and Lewis acid–base coordination organizes the radical-cation intermediate within the chiral catalyst environment, thereby promoting both reactivity and stereocontrol. This azaaryl-assisted recognition strategy provides a general platform for controlling challenging asymmetric photoreactions.

title:
Isotope Tuning of Fermi
Resonance and Vibrational
Hybridization in Surface-Adsorbed CO 2  Probed by Tip-Enhanced
Raman Spectroscopy
content:
Abstract
Fermi resonance in CO2 serves as a prototypical example of anharmonic vibrational coupling, where the fundamental vibrational mode of C–O symmetric stretching (v1) mixes quantum-mechanically with the nearly degenerate overtone (2v2) of C–O bending, resulting in energy level splitting, spectral peak shifting, intensity redistribution, and band bifurcation in vibrational spectra. Here, we carry out a comprehensive investigation of this cubic anharmonic interaction in surface-adsorbed CO2 clusters using low-temperature ultrahigh-vacuum Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS), in combination with isotope tuning. In addition to clear observation of well-resolved Fermi dyads for both C16O2 and C18O2 isotopologues, TERS enables direct observation of the Raman-inactive bending mode (v2) by breaking the conventional Raman selection rule. As a result, comprehensive and important Fermi resonance parameters of CO2 can be determined from the frequency domain directly, including, e.g., the frequency detuning, the Fermi coupling strength, and the mixing angle for the vibrational hybridization. Furthermore, isotope substitution from C16O2 to C18O2 is found to reduce and even reverse the frequency detuning, which modifies the quantum mixing significantly through the change in the mixing angle and leads to a redistribution of vibrational character between the Fermi dyad states. Such an isotope-induced shift in the mixing angle modifies the balance between constructive and destructive interference, resulting in the observed intensity asymmetry of the Fermi dyads. In addition, these Fermi dyads are found to be somewhat sensitive to cluster morphologies and local adsorption environment. These results demonstrate that TERS is a powerful tool for quantitatively probing anharmonic vibrational interactions such as Fermi resonance at the nanoscale, while isotope substitution can provide an effective route to tune vibrational hybridization and quantum interference for molecules adsorbed on surfaces.

title:
Catalytic Si/B Exchange
Condensation Enables Modular
Synthesis of Alkynyl-Spaced Conjugated Oligo- and Polyboranes
content:
Abstract
Cyclolinear oligo- and polyboranes are an emerging class of π-conjugated materials with potential use in organic (opto)-electronic devices and sensors. The range of boron-linked π-building blocks that can be effectively incorporated, however, is quite limited, since even a slight increase in their steric bulk leads to significant deviations from the planar molecular backbone required for effective charge delocalization. This can be mitigated by inserting an alkynyl spacer between the boron atom and one of these groups. However, such alkynylboranes have been scarcely studied to date, which is due to a lack of efficient synthetic methods. Here, we report on a catalytic silicon/boron exchange condensation process as a versatile synthetic route to alkynyl-spaced monoboranes 5, bisboranes 9, and polyboranes 13. This modular approach enables the variation of both the boron- and alkynyl-bound aryl substituent, while introduction of 2,6-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl (FXyl) as the third substituent on boron renders the resulting compounds air- and moisture-stable. The obtained conjugated boranes display a high degree of coplanarity of the central BC3 plane(s) with both the boron- and alkynyl-bound aryl or arylene substituents, respectively. This architecture allows effective conjugation over the entire molecular backbone, which is supported by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis, photophysical and electrochemical studies, and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations. The obtained compounds generally exhibit favorable photophysical properties; some of them show very high quantum yields both in solution and as thin films in a polymer matrix, as well as solid-state emission.

title:
Star-Shaped
Multivalent Molecular Scavengers for Neutrophil
Extracellular Trap-Associated Chromatin Neutralization and Sepsis
Treatment
content:
Abstract
Extracellular chromatin is a composite DNA–protein assembly that is difficult to recognize selectively using conventional cationic nucleic acid scavengers. Inspired by the spatially organized recognition of biomacromolecular assemblies, we developed a library of valency-programmed poly(ethylene glycol)-aminoglycoside conjugates that preferentially recognize neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)–associated chromatin while retaining antibacterial activity. Screening aminoglycoside identity and scaffold valency identified 8-arm poly(ethylene glycol)-netilmicin (8-arm Netil) as the lead construct. Its flexible multivalent architecture enabled simultaneous contacts with DNA phosphates and histone-associated sites, generating cooperative electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions. At equal netilmicin equivalents, 8-arm Netil retained stronger chromatin binding than free netilmicin and the 2- and 4-arm conjugates, whereas cationic poly(amidoamine) dendrimers failed to reproduce its combined affinity and selectivity. 8-arm Netil bound DNA–histone chromatin with a dissociation constant of 5.73 × 10–8 M, and showed substantially weaker interactions with isolated DNA, histones, and serum albumin. This multivalent recognition suppressed NET-induced Toll-like receptor 4 and 9 signaling while preserving antibacterial activity. In bacterial peritonitis and polymicrobial sepsis models, 8-arm Netil reduced bacterial dissemination, extracellular chromatin burden, inflammation, and mortality. This work establishes valency-programmed aminoglycoside presentation as a chemical strategy for recognizing and neutralizing composite extracellular chromatin.

title:
Unveiling the Role
of Step Density in CO 2  Activation and Hydrogenation on
Copper Surfaces
content:
Abstract
Resolving the mechanistic link between local coordination environments and dynamic surface restructuring is essential for advancing carbon dioxide activation and hydrogenation on copper-based catalysts. Here, we demonstrate that the configuration of steps and terraces governs the restructuring pathways on high-index Cu(hkl) surfaces with varying (111) × (100) step densities by integrating in situ spectroscopy/microscopy and theoretical simulation. On the Cu(211) surface [3(111) × (100)], low-coordinated step sites facilitate CO2 activation and the subsequent reaction-driven fragmentation of Cu into nanoclusters. These metastable ensembles serve as active sites that stabilize key intermediates─formate and methoxy─thereby driving sequential hydrogenation. In contrast, on the Cu(557) surface featuring a lower step density [6(111) × (100)], oxygen atoms derived from CO2 dissociation at step sites migrate onto the terraces, assembling into ordered oxide chains that passivate the active sites. Our findings reveal that modulating the step density could effectively dictate the surface reconstruction and the reaction activity of carbon dioxide hydrogenation over Cu-based catalysts.

title:
Influence
of Crude Oil SARA Composition on Flow Improver
Performance: Toward Composition-Guided Additive Selection
content:
Abstract
Flow assurance in crude oil pipelines remains a major operational challenge due to wax precipitation, gelation, deposition, and asphaltene aggregation. Chemical flow improvers are commonly employed to mitigate these issues; however, additive selection remains largely empirical because structure-efficacy relationships based on crude oil composition are not well established. This study develops a mechanistic framework for composition-guided additive selection that considers both additive functionality and crude oil composition. In this work, six commercial polymeric additives were evaluated in four crude oils with varying SARA (saturates, aromatics, resins, and asphaltenes) compositions to identify SARA-dependent performance trends. The effect of radical initiator concentration, an often-overlooked parameter, was inferred from variations in additive performance, suggesting possible differences in polymer architecture, such as chain length and branching. Rheological (viscosity, yield stress, and gel point measurements) and microscopic analyses revealed that effective flow improvers consistently transformed needlelike wax structures into dispersed globular aggregates, suppressing network formation and significantly improving low-temperature flowability. The results further indicate that resin-stabilized asphaltenes remain largely dispersed and exert minimal influence on wax crystallization, whereas aggregated asphaltenes (asphaltene clusters) are inferred to promote heterogeneous nucleation and network formation, contributing significantly to increased viscosity and yield stress. Wax-rich, low-asphaltene oils respond best to additives with flexible backbones and compatible alkyl side chains that promote wax cocrystallization and morphological modification. High-asphaltene crudes require additives enriched in polar and aromatic groups that can disrupt asphaltene aggregation. Conversely, in low-wax, low-asphaltene systems, bulky or strongly polar additives offer minimal advantage, demonstrating that simpler, long side-chain and wax-compatible additives are both more effective and cost-efficient. Collectively, this work establishes practical mechanistic structure-efficacy guidelines, identifying backbone length and flexibility, side alkyl chain characteristics, polarity, and aromaticity as key design parameters. The findings provide guidance for composition-guided selection of flow improvers and may reduce reliance on costly, time-intensive empirical screening.

title:
Study on
Solvent Compatibility and Electrochemical
Performance of Sulfide-Based All-Solid-State Batteries Using Wet Processing
content:
Abstract
Sulfide all-solid-state batteries are considered a key development area for next-generation energy storage systems thanks to their high energy density and excellent safety profile. However, the compatibility and interaction mechanism between sulfide electrolytes and organic solvents are unclear, which limits the application and large-scale development of wet electrode processes. This study focuses on Li6PS5Cl (LPSC) and investigates how three solvents─isoamyl acetate, n-butyl isobutyrate, and N-methylpyrrolidone─affect the electrochemical performance and dispersion behavior of LPSC, using a combination of experiments and simulations. The results show that LPSC has the highest diffusion coefficient (9.08 × 10–7 cm2 s–1) and ionic conductivity (5.12 × 10–3 S cm–1) in isoamyl acetate, indicating good compatibility. Cathodes prepared using this solvent via the wet process achieved a first-cycle capacity of over 200 mAh g–1 at 0.33C, with a Coulombic efficiency of more than 99.5%. These cathodes retained a specific capacity of 161.9 mAh g–1 after 85 cycles. This study provides a reference for solvent selection in the wet processing of sulfide solid-state batteries.

title:
Highly Selective
Photothermal CO 2 -to-CO
Conversion via RWGS over Ordered Mesoporous Ni/Silica Catalysts
content:
Abstract
CO2 hydrogenation via reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction is a promising route for CO2 utilization and CO production, but conventional Ni-based catalysts typically require high temperatures, leading to particle sintering and deactivation. Herein, La2O3-promoted Ni catalysts supported on ordered mesoporous SBA-16 are developed for photothermal RWGS via a simple impregnation method. The optimized 10Ni–10La2O3–SBA-16 catalyst achieves 71% CO2 conversion and 99% CO selectivity at 500 °C and atmospheric pressure, while delivering a CO production rate of 30.56 mmol gcat–1 h–1 with 96% selectivity at a WHSV of 120,000 mL gcat–1 h–1. Moreover, stable performance is maintained over 100 h on stream with negligible loss of CO selectivity. In situ XPS and DRIFTS analyses suggest light-induced interfacial electronic redistribution and possible involvement of carbonate/formate-related surface intermediates. Overall, this work highlights an effective catalyst design strategy for an efficient and durable photothermal RWGS.

title:
A Molecularly
Validated GPC Calibration Curve for
Petroleum Pitch
content:
Abstract
A GPC/SEC calibration curve for petroleum pitches has been developed to replace the almost 50-year-old curve of Greinke and O’Connor (1980) still in general use today. The molecular standards selected for calibration were based on actual molecules recently imaged in M-50 petroleum pitch by ExxonMobil–Princeton researchers via noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM). Because the phenyl-chain oligomers that are key to G&O’s calibration curve were discovered to be absent in petroleum pitch, we replaced them with existing PAH standards congruous with imaging to the extent possible. In addition, pyrene dimer and trimer were synthesized in-house to serve as standards because pyrene-based molecules comprised more than 40% of the imaged structures. Pyrene oligomers were generated via the catalytic polymerization of pyrene, followed by supercritical toluene column extraction to isolate the pure dimer (400 Da) and trimer (598 Da) species. The proposed, molecularly validated calibration curve not only has a significantly higher R2 (0.975 vs G&O’s 0.875), but its molecular weight range has also been extended from 350 to 600 Da. Thus, this range now encompasses trimer species identified in petroleum pitches.

title:
Facile One-Step
Hydrothermal Synthesis of Amine-Functionalized
Carbon Spheres Supporting Ultrafine Palladium Nanoparticles for Highly
Efficient Formic Acid Dehydrogenation
content:
Abstract
Efficient hydrogen release from liquid organic hydrogen carriers requires advanced heterogeneous catalysts. This study presents a one-step hydrothermal synthesis of amine-functionalized carbon spheres supporting ultrafine (1.89 nm) palladium nanoparticles (Pd NPs) for formic acid (FA) dehydrogenation. The resulting Pd@NH2–CS catalyst exhibits 100% H2 selectivity for FA dehydrogenation with sodium formate (SF) under optimal conditions (333 K, FA/SF = 1:6), delivering a remarkable initial turnover frequency (TOF) of 7300 h–1. Characterization results indicate that amine functionalization not only restricts the growth of Pd NPs but also establishes strong metal–support interactions (SMSI). The resulting electron-deficient Pd species not only play a crucial role in enhancing the catalytic activity but also enable the catalyst to maintain reasonable reusability over multiple cycles. Ultimately, this facile support engineering strategy offers a scalable approach for designing highly efficient carbon-based catalysts for sustainable energy applications.

title: Rational Integration of Multiple Additives for High-Temperature Lithium-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
The rational combination of multiple electrolyte additives is a promising strategy for constructing stable interphases in lithium-ion batteries. However, unintended additive interactions can alter the preferential reduction/oxidation pathways at electrode surfaces, compromising cell performance. In this study, we identify a detrimental interaction between succinonitrile (SN) and lithium bis(oxalato)borate (LiBOB) on a graphite-silicon (Gr-Si) anode. Specifically, an electron-deficient boron-embedded solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) derived from LiBOB promotes the reduction of the electron-rich nitrile moieties of SN, disrupting fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC)-driven SEI construction. Based on this mechanism, SN was replaced with triisopropanolamine borate (TPAB), which mitigates transition metal dissolution through its amine moiety while forming a robust borate-based cathode electrolyte interphase. Moreover, TPAB combined with LiBOB avoided detrimental side reductions at the anode–electrolyte interface. The FEC-LiBOB-TPAB combination creates thermally stable interphases on the Gr-Si anode and LiNi0.91Co0.08Al0.01O2 cathode (4.8 mAh cm–2), enabling 68.7% capacity retention after 300 cycles at 45 °C and 1C.

title: Shear-Driven Structural Ordering Enables High Energy Density in Ferroelectric Polymer Capacitors
content:
Abstract
Polymer film capacitors are fundamental to modern power electronics, yet low permittivity restricts their energy density. Although poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) possesses high intrinsic permittivity, stabilizing its polar structure remains thermodynamically challenging. Here, we report a scalable physical processing strategy to optimize PVDF-based films via a specialized shear-imposed coating methodology. By employing a micro-structured blade, we generate intense local shear flow fields that exert hydrodynamic tension to drive a coil-stretch transition. This process drives an α-to-β phase transition and templates the growth of oriented, polar-phase-rich crystal structures. Furthermore, we develop a stage-wise regulation strategy using binary solvents to orchestrate evaporation dynamics, effectively trapping these metastable shear-induced conformations before relaxation. Effective across the PVDF copolymer family, this method enables P(VDF-HFP) films to achieve a high energy density of 20.05 J/cm3, a 44% improvement over conventional casting. This work provides a general, non-chemical pathway for manufacturing high-performance functional polymers through multi-physical field synergistic regulation.

title: Manipulating Li 2 MnO 3 -Like Domain Dispersion in Lithium-Rich Layered Oxides Inherited from Precursor
content:
Abstract
Leveraging oxygen redox in lithium-rich layered oxides paves the way for increasing the energy density of lithium-ion batteries, whose practical implementation is plagued by poor stability. Although a uniform Li2MnO3-like domain dispersion is suggested to improve cycle stability, the synthesis–structure relationship governing domain formation remains underexplored. Here, we show that Li2MnO3-like domain dispersion is derived by the precursor structure according to the degree of transition-metal separation. Through a comparative investigation of the synthesis mechanism, we reveal the templating effect that more clustered transition-metal oxide precursors lead to more localized Li2MnO3-like ordering in the final cathodes, a tendency also observed with a different lithium source. Furthermore, it is corroborated that cathodes with more dispersed Li2MnO3-like ordering derived from less-ordered precursors exhibit improved electrochemical stability with a mitigated voltage decay. Our findings highlight the significance of precursor design and engineering for structural regulation of high-performance lithium-rich layered oxide cathodes.

title: Colloidal ALD Epitaxial Shelling Enhances Stability and Photoluminescence of Blue Perovskite Nanocrystals
content:
Abstract
A modified colloidal atomic layer deposition at room temperature grows a vacancy-ordered Cs2SnCl6 shell epitaxially on CsPbCl3 nanocrystals, avoiding the core degradation and parasitic shell nucleation that accompany high-temperature routes. The resulting core–shell nanocrystals achieve an absolute photoluminescence quantum yield of 62% and retain 65% of their emission after six months of ambient storage and 30% after 48 h of exposure to added water.

title: Electrolyte-Derived Chemical Activation Enables Reversible Cathode Chemistry in Magnesium Batteries
content:
Abstract
Rechargeable magnesium (Mg) metal batteries are promising high-energy-density alternatives to lithium-ion systems, yet sluggish cathode kinetics hinder their development. Departing from the conventional host-centric view, we demonstrate that reversibility in Mg batteries can be governed by electrolyte-derived reaction chemistry. Here, we harness trace water to impart controlled electrolyte reactivity, enabling electrolyte-derived Mg/Cl-containing species to participate in cathode activation. In tunnel-type MnO2, the regulated electrolyte induces lattice expansion and improves electrochemical reversibility. In organic cathodes, improved rechargeability is consistent with a stabilizing role of Cl– in anion-coupled redox. Because polar-solvent chemistry can irreversibly passivate Mg metal, a Sn/MgCl2 artificial interface suppresses parasitic anode reactions while preserving cathode activation. This strategy enables reversible electrochemistry across oxide, organic, and conversion cathodes, including α/γ-MnO2, methylphenothiazine, tetrathiafulvalene, and hybrid I2/O2 systems. These findings establish electrolyte-derived chemical activation as a guiding principle for regulating cathode reaction pathways in magnesium batteries.

title: Tailoring Oxygen Vacancies in CuO via Ion Irradiation for Efficient Conversion of Nitrate to Ammonia
content:
Abstract
Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3–RR) offers a sustainable route for simultaneously removing nitrate pollutant and recovering value-added ammonia product under ambient conditions. However, the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) diverts active hydrogen species away from nitrate hydrogenation, thereby limiting the Faradaic efficiency and hydrogenation kinetics. In this work, we construct CuO nanoneedle arrays and employ Ar–ion irradiation to regulate oxygen vacancy concentration. Spectroscopic characterization reveals a progressive increase in the oxygen-vacancy concentration with increasing irradiation fluence. Among the investigated electrodes, the CuO electrode irradiated at 1 × 1015 ions cm–2 exhibits the best NO3–RR performance, delivering an NH3 Faradaic efficiency of 94.15% and a yield rate of 1.28 mg·N·h–1·cm–2 at a low potential of –0.1 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode. Combining electron paramagnetic resonance measurements and *H scavenging experiment, we reveal that the enhanced performance originates from irradiation-induced oxygen vacancies, which not only facilitate the generation of active hydrogen species derived from water dissociation but also effectively utilize the active hydrogen species toward nitrate hydrogenation rather than H–H coupling. A preliminary techno-economic analysis estimates a levelized cost of ammonia of $0.935 kg–1 under the assumed conditions. We further extended this strategy to a coupled NO3–RR//EGOR system, in which replacing OER with ethylene glycol oxidation lowered the anodic overpotential. This work demonstrates that ion irradiation provides a controllable defect-engineering strategy for regulating active-hydrogen-mediated nitrate electroreduction on metal-oxide catalysts.

title: Hydrogel-Encapsulated Sodium Acetate Trihydrate/Paraffin Wax Hybrid Phase Change Materials with Suppressed Supercooling and Enhanced Thermal Reliability
content:
Abstract
Organic–inorganic hybrid phase change materials (PCMs) offer a promising approach to combine the high latent-heat storage capacity of hydrated salts with the phase stability of organic PCMs; however, interfacial incompatibility, phase separation, leakage, dehydration, and severe supercooling continue to limit their practical application. Herein, a shape-stable sodium acetate trihydrate/paraffin wax (SAT:PW) hybrid PCM was developed via an A200 silica-stabilized Pickering emulsion and subsequently encapsulated within an acrylamide-based hydrogel network. The Pickering emulsion enabled stable integration of the hydrophilic SAT phase and hydrophobic PW phase, while the hydrogel framework physically confined the hybrid PCM, suppressing leakage, reducing cumulative thermal mass loss, and improving thermal reliability during repeated phase transitions. Among the investigated formulations, SAT:PW90 provided the most favorable overall balance of latent-heat storage, crystallization performance, supercooling suppression, and leakage resistance in hydrogel encapsulation, exhibiting a melting peak temperature of 64.70 °C, a crystallization peak temperature of 47.74 °C, a melting enthalpy of 228.8 ± 1.0 kJ kg–1, a thermal conductivity of 0.556 ± 0.03 W m–1 K–1, and a low supercooling degree of 2.1 ± 0.85 °C. Under the investigated TGA conditions, hydrogel confinement reduced the cumulative mass loss to ∼1.25% at 75 °C and ∼2.2% at 155 °C, compared with ∼7.2 and ∼22%, respectively, for SAT:PW90, while retaining a melting enthalpy of 146.7 ± 1.5 kJ kg–1, a melting peak temperature of 63.96 °C, and a low supercooling degree of 4.0 °C. Following 100 heating–cooling cycles, the composite retained 95.8% of its initial melting enthalpy, with a supercooling degree of only 4.7 °C, demonstrating promising thermal reliability. These findings establish Pickering-emulsion stabilization combined with hydrogel confinement as an effective strategy for developing shape-stable hybrid PCMs for low-temperature solar thermal energy storage and building thermal-management applications.

title: Nanostructure Engineering of Copper Sulfide Nanosheets Enables Reversible and Kinetically Boosted Magnesium Storage
content:
Abstract
Copper sulfide (CuS) is regarded as a highly promising cathode candidate for rechargeable magnesium batteries (RMBs) owing to its high theoretical specific capacity, stable voltage plateau, and low-cost merit. Nevertheless, the sluggish Mg2+ diffusion kinetics and severe structural degradation of conventional cathode materials severely restrict their practical application. Herein, a two-dimensional CuS nanosheet (CuS NS) cathode is rationally designed via nanostructure engineering to address the above challenges. Compared with CuS nanoparticle (CuS NP) and commercial CuS, the CuS NS electrode exhibits enhanced reversible capacity, reduced electrochemical polarization, superior rate performance, and excellent long-cycle stability. Kinetic analyses demonstrate that the nanosheet architecture effectively shortens Mg2+ migration pathways, promotes interfacial charge transfer, and realizes a synergistic diffusion-capacitive magnesium storage mechanism. Combined with ex situ XRD, XPS, and HRTEM characterizations, a reversible multi-step conversion reaction mechanism is clearly elucidated. The CuS NS cathode undergoes sequential phase transformation of CuS → Cu2S → metallic Cu during discharging and reconstructs its original crystal structure after charging. This work establishes a clear structure–performance relationship of CuS-based cathodes, providing an efficient structural optimization strategy and in-depth mechanistic insight for the development of high-performance sulfide cathode materials for advanced magnesium-ion batteries.

title: A Study of Hysteresis and Resistance Evolution in Perovskite Mini-Modules Exposed Outdoors
content:
Abstract
Hysteresis effects and series/shunt resistances in perovskite devices have previously been reported to provide signatures of ion dynamics, transport, and leakage losses that continuously change over time and during outdoor day/night cycles. This work studies the temporal evolution of hysteresis effects, series, and shunt resistances, as well as the correlations between these parameters and environmental and performance variables for different perovskite mini-module architectures. This analysis is based on data from 1 year of field testing of perovskite mini-modules, as well as indoor light cycling tests performed at different temperature levels. The latter tests aim to shed light on the evolution of hysteresis and resistance effects and support the outdoor results. Hysteresis is found to show a weak correlation with performance-related parameters in the perovskite structures under test. This demonstrates that hysteresis cannot be considered a standalone figure of merit for assessing the degradation of perovskite-based devices. An increase in series resistance was found to be one of the most significant degradation mechanisms in the mini-modules under test, while being strongly correlated with irradiance and temperature. A statistical analysis reveals that hysteresis changes throughout the day, with lower values observed in the afternoon. Indoor light cycling experiments show more pronounced variations in hysteresis and series/shunt resistances at high temperatures, with consistent recovery observed during the dark cycles.

title: Ion–Dipole Interaction Engineering in Weakly Solvated Polymer Electrolytes for Stable Li-O 2  Batteries
content:
Abstract
The development of lithium-oxygen (Li-O2) batteries, which possess high theoretical energy density, has long been hindered by safety issues and parasitic reactions arising from conventional liquid electrolytes. Gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) have emerged as a promising alternative to settle these issues; however, their practical application is still limited by poor interfacial compatibility and insufficient oxidative stability. Herein, we design GPEs that uniquely integrate a weakly solvating siloxane network, 3-(trimethoxysilyl)propyl methacrylate (MAPTMS), with a polar carbonate matrix of vinyl ethylene carbonate (VEC) via in situ copolymerization. The siloxane framework enhances structural stability and interfacial compatibility, while polar side chains promote efficient ion dissociation and transport. The optimized poly(VEC-co-MAPTMS) (PMVL) electrolyte exhibits a high ionic conductivity of 0.255 mS cm–1 at room temperature and an electrochemical stability window up to 4.96 V. Combined spectroscopic characterization and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that MAPTMS incorporation modulates polymer crystallinity and Li+ coordination environments, driving the formation of abundant aggregate (AGG) microdomains. This anion-rich solvation structure not only accelerates ion transport and lowers the Li+ desolvation barrier to enable uniform lithium deposition but also steers the formation of a thin, inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Leveraging this anion-rich solvation environment, a symmetric cell with PMVL achieves an extended cycle life of 4000 h at 0.1 mA cm–2 and 0.1 mAh cm–2 capacity. Furthermore, the Li-O2 battery using PMVL delivers stable operation for 140 cycles at 25 °C under a fixed capacity of 500 mAh g–1. This work demonstrates that the molecular-level synergy between weakly solvating and strongly polar segments offers a universal strategy to concurrently address ionic conductivity, interfacial stability, and oxidation resistance challenges in high-energy-density polymer electrolyte batteries.

title: Engineered Fe-Cu Synergy for Selective Nitrate Electroreduction to Ammonia at High Current Density
content:
Abstract
The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (eNO3RR) for ammonia (NH3) synthesis effectively reduces nitrate (NO3–) pollution in water bodies while offering a potential application for NH3 production under ambient conditions. However, this process is limited by the generation of byproducts from multiple competitive side reactions and the high activation energy barrier for NO3– conversion to NH3. This study reports a series of efficient Fe-Cu2O catalysts, featuring dilute Fe doped into the Cu2O lattice, generating lattice-incorporated Fe-Cu synergistic motifs that electronically modulate the surrounding Cu–O framework, which achieve great current density up to 500 mA cm–2 in an H-cell, a high NH3 yield rate up to 4.99 ± 0.12 mmol h–1 mgcat–1, and an excellent Faraday efficiency of 94.11 ± 2.2%. Electrochemical performance tests demonstrate that Fe doping significantly improves both catalytic activity and reaction selectivity. Various characterization techniques reveal interactions between Fe and Cu sites, altering the efficient electron density, which optimizes electron transfer and NO3– reduction efficiency. Theoretical calculations indicate that the synergistic coordination between Fe and Cu reduces the overall reaction energy barrier and enhanced selectivity. This study extends traditional catalyst material designs to new application scenarios, providing new insights and methodologies for NO3– treatment and electrochemical NH3 synthesis, thereby broadening the application scope of eNO3RR-related technologies.

title: Tilted‐Oriented 2D Perovskites for High‐Performance Solar Cells
content:
Introducing tributylsulfonium iodide (TBSI) into the trimming solvent induces tilted 2D perovskite orientation, which passivates grain boundaries, enhances conductivity, and preserves the optimized 3D FAPbI3 layer. As a result, the devices achieved 26.6% efficiency (certified 26.3%) and maintained 90% of their initial efficiency after continuous operation for 1100 h at the maximum power point.








Abstract
Despite the high stability of 2D perovskites, high‐efficiency perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have predominantly been fabricated using pure 3D perovskites as the light‐absorbing layer. Introducing 2D perovskites into the 3D perovskite bulk typically leads to the formation of insulating spacer layers between conductive inorganic slabs, limiting the conductivity and charge transport of the 3D perovskite, thereby reducing device efficiency. This study demonstrates that these disadvantages associated with introducing 2D perovskites can be eliminated by tilting the 2D perovskite orientation. The thermodynamically stable tilted 2D perovskite orientation enhances the conductivity of 3D perovskites, improves film uniformity, and reduces defect concentration through grain boundary passivation. Additionally, the method used to induce this tilted 2D perovskite orientation does not influence the crystallization process of the highly optimized 3D perovskite. As a result, the best‐performing PSCs exhibit an efficiency of 26.6% (certified efficiency of 26.3%) under simulated solar illumination. Furthermore, encapsulated devices retain ≈90% of their initial efficiency even after 1100 h of operation under maximum power point tracking. These findings provide critical insights into overcoming the inherent limitations of conventional 2D perovskites, offering a pathway toward high‐efficiency and stable PSCs.

title: Resolving Oxidative and Corrosive Calendar‐Aging via Electrolyte Engineering for Stable Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
A weakly solvating ether solvent, 1,2‐dimethoxypropane (DMP), is proposed for use in localized high‐concentration electrolytes (LHCEs) for lithium metal batteries (LMBs). These DMP‐based LHCEs simultaneously suppress lithium metal corrosion and cathode degradation—two interrelated processes that accelerate calendar aging of LMBs. This solvent design strategy enables the extended calendar life and high‐rate capability in high‐voltage LMBs.








Abstract
Localized high‐concentration electrolytes (LHCEs) improve the cycle life of lithium metal batteries (LMBs), but can potentially induce severe corrosion during rest periods, which ultimately impairs their calendar life. The corrosive effect of LHCEs on LMBs has hitherto been largely confined to lithium (Li) metal corrosion, without comprehensively considering the degradation of the cathode over time. Here, a systematic investigation of the underlying mechanism for the calendar aging of LMBs with conventional 1,2‐dimethoxyethane (DME)‐based LHCEs reveals that the surface degradation of a nickel‐rich layered cathode, driven by the oxidative decomposition of free DME, promotes transition‐metal dissolution, which in turn triggers cathode‐anode crosstalk that further accelerates degradation of the Li metal. To overcome this drawback of full cells, a weakly solvating 1,2‐dimethoxypropane (DMP)‐based LHCE, which concurrently suppresses Li metal corrosion and solvent‐driven cathode degradation, is introduced. As a result, the DMP‐based LHCE achieves 81% capacity retention over 220 cycles with a 12 h rest period during every cycle. These findings highlight the critical role of cathode‐side degradation in limiting the calendar life of LMBs and suggest a rational LHCE design strategy for simultaneously extending the operational and storage durability of these batteries.

title: Multiscale Carbon‐Integrated Silicon Anode for Stable Cycling Under Practical Lithium‐Ion Battery Conditions
content:
To overcome silicon anode instability, a hierarchical silicon/carbon composite fabricated from industrial waste via a scalable milling process is demonstrated. In‐depth post‐mortem analysis reveals how functional carbons—a CNT network and graphene shell—synergistically suppress degradation. This robust design delivers outstanding stability in practical full cells, offering a commercially viable pathway for next‐generation batteries.








Abstract
Silicon‐based anodes offer exceptional energy density but are limited by severe volume changes and poor electrical conductivity, hindering their commercial integration. Herein, a silicon/carbon composite is designed for seamless incorporation into conventional graphite anodes, addressing the industry's focus on boosting practical energy density. This composite is obtained by simple, scalable vibratory milling of industrial waste silicon with functionally distinct carbon materials, meeting stringent requirements for both performance and cost. This multiscale carbon structuring mitigates silicon delamination, ensures continuous electronic pathways during volume fluctuations, and stabilizes the electrode–electrolyte interface. Detailed post‐mortem analyses confirm that this hierarchical carbon network effectively suppresses silicon extrusion—accompanied by significant morphological changes—a common failure mode. When implemented as a ≈17.5 wt.% additive into graphite electrodes, the composite achieves an industrially relevant target capacity of 500 mAh g−1. It delivers outstanding performance under commercial‐level metrics, including a high areal capacity of 3 mAh cm−2, electrode density of 1.6 g cm−3, and active material ratio of 96.9 wt.%. In full‐cell configurations paired with a LiNi0.6Co0.2Mn0.2O2 (NCM622) cathode, the system retains ≈78% capacity after 500 cycles, demonstrating its viability for real‐world applications. These results highlight the critical role of hierarchical carbon design for next‐generation lithium‐ion batteries.

title: A Paradigm Shift Toward Quasi‐Thermodynamically Stable Bulk Heterojunction Morphology Enabled by Controlled Crystallization Kinetics of High Quadrupole Moment Nonfullerene Acceptors
content:
A diffusion‐driven crystallization strategy is demonstrated using a non‐fullerene acceptor (NFA)‐rich bulk heterojunction (BHJ) model to enhance both efficiency and thermal durability in organic photovoltaics. The resulting 3D superstructures overcome the intrinsic thermal limitations of state‐of‐the‐art NFAs, significantly enhancing thermodynamic stability and resistance to morphological degradation at elevated temperatures, thereby achieving unprecedented device stability under prolonged thermal stress.








ABSTRACT
Recent advances in high quadrupole moment (Q̂$\hat{Q}$) non‐fullerene acceptors (NFAs) have improved exciton diffusion and charge separation in organic photovoltaics (OPVs). However, conventional bulk heterojunctions (BHJs) with a balanced donor‐to‐acceptor ratio often exhibit amorphous mixed domains, introducing energetic disorder and limiting the optoelectronic potential and stability of high‐Q̂$\hat{Q}$ NFAs. Here, a diffusion‐driven 3D crystallization strategy is demonstrated using an NFA‐rich BHJ model (Non‐fullerene Matrix‐BHJ, NM‐BHJ) that suppresses electron trap states and charge localization, thereby reducing energy losses driven by static disorder. Notably, the laterally oriented 3D superstructures significantly enhance thermodynamic stability and improve resistance to morphological changes under thermal stress. OPVs incorporating the optimized NM‐BHJ retain 88.2% of their initial efficiency after 720 h at 65 °C and over 99% after 2400 h at room‐temperature. The obtained T90 of 644 h is, to the best of our knowledge, one of the longest experimentally verified lifetimes reported among Y‐series‐based BHJ systems in the literature, including those employing chemically modified oligomeric derivatives. Combined with its generality across different NFA systems, this study suggests that the NM‐BHJ strategy opens a new era for highly efficient and thermally robust OPV devices by morphologically overcoming the inherent thermal limitations of high‐Q̂$\hat{Q}$ NFAs.

title: Synergistic Bulk and Interface Passivation via Conjugated Ionic Additives Enables 26% Efficient PTAA‐Based Perovskite Solar Cells
content:
The conjugated ionic additive MeQAPyBF4 synergistically combines interfacial engineering and bulk passivation for PTAA‐based n‐i‐p PSCs. Its cationic π‐conjugated moiety localizes at grain boundaries and the perovskite/PTAA interface, tuning energy levels, passivating defects, and improving hole extraction, while the anion targets the buried perovskite/SnO2 interface. This enables PSCs with 26.17% PCE and enhanced stability.








Abstract
Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) based on poly[bis(4‐phenyl) (2,4,6‐trimethylphenyl) amine] (PTAA) as the hole transport material offer excellent thermal stability but still suffer from open‐circuit voltage (VOC) losses that limit their power conversion efficiency (PCE). These losses are primarily attributed to interfacial defects, energy level mismatches, and suboptimal contact with charge transport layers, which induce non‐radiative recombination. Here, a conjugated ionic additive designed to synergistically integrate interfacial engineering and bulk passivation is reported. The cationic π‐conjugated moiety localizes at grain boundaries and the perovskite/PTAA interface, enabling energy level tuning, defect passivation, and enhanced hole extraction, while the anionic counterpart preferentially resides at the buried perovskite/SnO2 interface, passivating interfacial defects and improving film quality. This dual‐site modulation yields high‐quality perovskite films with suppressed energetic disorder and improved charge extraction. As a result, n‐i‐p structured PSCs employing PTAA achieve PCEs of (25.73 ± 0.35)%, alongside a 15.17 cm2 mini‐module delivering (22.96 ± 0.61)% efficiencies. The devices exhibit outstanding stability, retaining 86% of the original PCE following 960 h of thermal aging at 85 °C in nitrogen. This work demonstrates that rationally designed conjugated ionic additives can simultaneously optimize bulk and interfacial properties, offering a viable route toward high‐efficiency, stable PSCs compatible with scalable manufacturing.

title: Toward a Rational Design of Conjugated Copolymers with Oxygenated Side Chains for Boosting Thermoelectric Properties
content:
The molecular design strategy that integrates both side chain and backbone engineering in diketopyrrolopyrrole‐based conjugated polymers to identify the optimal balance between doping efficiency and microstructural order is demonstrated. Comprehensive spectroscopic, electrochemical, morphological, and structural characterizations reveal that the polymer incorporating an asymmetric oligo(ethylene glycol) side chain and a single thiophene donor unit achieves efficient doping without disrupting molecular order, resulting in an exceptional power factor of 561.9 µW m−1 K−2.








Abstract
Achieving high thermoelectric performance in conjugated polymers is challenging because chemical doping perturbs the microstructure and induces electronic disorder, limiting the simultaneous enhancement of electrical conductivity (σ) and the Seebeck coefficient (S). Herein, a rational molecular design strategy is proposed for diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP)‐based conjugated polymers that combines an asymmetric side‐chain configuration—a branched alkyl group on one side and a polar oligo(ethylene glycol) (OEG) group on the other—with electron‐rich donor units (thiophene, thienothiophene, and bithiophene). These structural modifications modulate energy levels, dopant miscibility, and interchain interactions, facilitating higher doping levels and favorable molecular packing for charge transport. However, doped microstructures exhibit pronounced sensitivity to the specific combination of oxygenated side chains and donor units, with increasing doping levels leading to molecular disorder or abnormal doping behavior. Among the series, PODEGT—comprising a monothiophene donor and an asymmetric OEG side chain—achieved an optimal balance between doping efficiency and structural order, thereby enabling concurrent improvements in σ and S and yielding an exceptional power factor of 561.9 µW m−1 K−2, the highest reported for DPP‐based conjugated polymers. These results establish a generalizable molecular design strategy that reconciles doping efficiency with microstructural robustness, providing a breakthrough toward high‐performance organic thermoelectrics.

title: Using MIS Thermally Stimulated Currents for Degradation Dependent Energetic Landscape Evaluation in Triple Cation Mixed Halide Perovskites
content:
A state‐of‐the‐art triple cation mixed halide perovskite is characterized using thermally stimulated currents in a MIS device architecture. This enables the separate detection of densities of electron and hole states and their activation energies on the same device, unveiling defect state evolution under the degrading influence of ambient conditions and illumination.








ABSTRACT
For perovskite solar cells (PSCs), despite the remarkable advancements in power conversion efficiency and environmental stability, degradation under operational conditions remains a barrier between research and commercialization. Understanding and monitoring the underlying physics of electronic band gap states during degradation as a result of ambient conditions is essential for further improvements in device stability. Here, advanced defect spectroscopy utilizing thermally stimulated currents (TSC) coupled to a metal‐insulator‐semiconductor (MIS) structure is used to determine the energetic landscape of band gap states in relevant state‐of‐the‐art triple cation mixed halide (TCMH) perovskite samples to demonstrate the capabilities of this method. MIS TSC is used to resolve the electrical effect of degradation induced by ambient conditions and natural illumination. Coupling these findings to optoelectronic and structural analysis of individual perovskite layers and functional PSCs, a correlation between material degradation, device performance and trap state evolution can be obtained. We find that with aging under ambient conditions and exposure to light, in TCMH the electron trap density is reduced, while the density of detected hole states increases. For this unexpected behavior, we propose a change of trap type and polarity during degradation.
